plan.contextChunk: This figure contains five panels (a)–(e) tracing the execution of the Bellman-Ford algorithm on a directed weighted graph with five vertices s, t, x, y, and z and ten directed edges with weights 6, 7, 5, 8, −4, −2, −3, 9, 7, and 2. The same graph layout is used in all five panels: vertex s appears at the left, t and y in the center-left region, and x and z at the right; each vertex circle displays the current shortest-path estimate d[v] inside it. Panel (a) shows the initial state with d[s] = 0 and d[v] = ∞ for all other vertices, and all edges drawn as thin black arrows labeled with their weights. Panels (b) through (e) each show the graph after one additional relaxation pass; bold gray arrows highlight the edges whose relaxation improved a distance estimate in that pass, and updated d[v] values appear inside the affected vertex circles. After pass 1 (panel b), d[t] = 6 and d[y] = 7. After pass 2 (panel c), d[x] = 4 and d[z] = 2. After pass 3 (panel d), d[t] = 2 and d[z] = −2. Panel (e) shows the final shortest-path estimates d[s] = 0, d[t] = 2, d[x] = 4, d[y] = 7, d[z] = −2, with bold arrows forming the shortest-path tree along the path s → y → x → t → z. This figure demonstrates the Bellman-Ford algorithm's iterative relaxation process, showing how negative-weight edges cause distance estimates to decrease over successive passes until convergence.

interactionPlan.concept: Bellman-Ford finds shortest paths by repeatedly relaxing every directed edge, allowing distance estimates to propagate one edge farther per pass and to decrease again when negative-weight edges become reachable.

interactions.frame: Each recorded frame shows the whole five-vertex directed graph, the active edge being relaxed, the candidate value dist[u] + w, all current distance labels, predecessor highlights, the pass number, and the number of successful distance updates in that pass.

input.label: Fixed Bellman-Ford instance
input.default: Initial distances: s=0, t=x=y=z=∞. Run 4 passes over edges in this order: t→x 5, t→y 8, t→z −4, x→t −2, y→x −3, y→z 9, z→x 7, z→s 2, s→t 6, s→y 7.

interactions.success_check: After 4 passes the distances must be dist.s = 0, dist.t = 2, dist.x = 4, dist.y = 7, dist.z = −2, with predecessor edges s→y, y→x, x→t, and t→z forming the final shortest-path tree.
interactions.teaches: A correct relaxation step locally compares one candidate path against the current estimate; repeated in edge-order passes, these local updates propagate shortest-path information through the graph until the final predecessor tree emerges

demo_steps.title: Initialize estimates
demo_steps.narration: The source vertex s starts at distance 0, while every other vertex starts at ∞ because no paths from s have been discovered yet. All edges are present, but no predecessor tree exists.

demo_steps.title: Pass 1: discover neighbors of s
demo_steps.narration: During the first full edge pass, only the late relaxations s→t and s→y improve distances, producing d[t]=6 and d[y]=7. The first gray predecessor edges show the best known one-edge paths from s.

demo_steps.title: Pass 2: propagate through t and y
demo_steps.narration: Now that t and y have finite estimates, their outgoing edges can improve other vertices. The algorithm reaches x with final estimate 4 through y→x and reaches z with estimate 2 through t→z.

demo_steps.title: Pass 3: a negative edge lowers t
demo_steps.narration: Because x is now known to have distance 4, relaxing x→t with weight −2 improves t from 6 down to 2. This shows why Bellman-Ford must keep making passes even after a vertex already has a finite estimate.

demo_steps.title: Pass 4: final improvement reaches z
demo_steps.narration: With t improved to 2, the next pass relaxes t→z with weight −4 and lowers z to −2. The final predecessor chain s→y→x→t→z is the shortest-path tree.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Bellman-Ford works because each pass lets improved estimates travel one more edge along a shortest path, so even negative edges are handled as long as repeated relaxation is allowed to converge.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Use the same five-node layout as the textbook figure: s on the far left, t above y near the center, and x above z on the right. Draw all edges as thin black arrows with clear weight labels, including the paired curved arrows between t and x. Show distance estimates inside light-gray circular nodes. During code replay, flash the active edge; when relaxation succeeds, place a thick gray backing under that edge and update the destination node's number. Maintain a persistent gray predecessor-tree overlay after each successful update so the learner can see the evolving tree: first s→t and s→y, then y→x and t→z, then x→t replaces s→t, and finally t→z leads to z=−2. Include a pass/change counter beside the graph rather than recreating five static panels at once.

discrepancies: the default view shows only panel (a) with a large control/code panel beside it, whereas the source is a five-panel static sequence arranged in a 3-over-2 layout

extra annotations such as 'initial estimates', pass/change text, active-edge/candidate labels, and the guided-demo UI are not present in the source and make the figure look less like the textbook image
edge-weight labels are placed on white rectangular backplates, unlike the source's plain text labels, and these backplates slightly alter the visual character of the graph
the highlighted predecessor edges in the stepped panels are rendered as very thick gray bands with an extra active-edge emphasis, stronger and less uniform than the source's gray highlights
evaluation.notes: The graph topology, weights, vertex estimates, and Bellman-Ford progression are highly accurate, but the generated version is an interactive single-panel teaching demo rather than a close visual reproduction of the full five-panel textbook figure.
action_items: Provide a static overview mode or thumbnail/composite mode that displays panels (a)–(e) in the same 3-over-2 arrangement as the source.
Reduce or hide non-source annotations such as pass/change text and active-candidate labels in the default textbook-replacement view.
Remove the white rectangular label backplates or make them much subtler so edge labels match the source's plain typography.
Tune the gray predecessor highlights to be closer to the source: slightly thinner, more uniform, and less dominated by the active-edge overlay.

feedback.rationale: The concept and data are accurate, but the default rendering and extra UI/annotation styling diverge from the source, so the generator should refine layout and visual presentation rather than revising the plan.

discrepancies: The default rendered output is dominated by a large right-side guided demo/code-editor UI that is not present in the source figure, so it is not a clean drop-in replacement for the static textbook image.

The five Bellman-Ford panels are compressed into the left half of the viewport; compared with the source, all nodes, edge labels, vertex labels, and panel captions are much smaller and harder to read.

The overview panel spacing and scale differ substantially from the source: the reference uses the full width for the three top panels and two larger bottom panels, while the generated figure leaves most visual area to controls.
Some exterior vertex labels, especially the left-side s labels in the overview, sit very close to the edge and feel cramped compared with the source.

The generated figure adds instructional status text, narration, run controls, and code-workbench elements that change the visual composition even though the graph panels themselves are mostly faithful.
evaluation.notes: The Bellman-Ford graph topology, edge weights, estimates, and gray predecessor bands are very accurate, but the default view is heavily scaled down and visually displaced by a large interactive UI.
action_items: Make the default overview prioritize the textbook figure: give the SVG nearly the full available width and collapse or dock the code/demo UI below or behind a toggle.
Increase overview scale and text sizes so vertex labels, edge weights, node values, and panel captions are comfortably readable at inline size.
Add more left/right padding around each mini-panel so exterior labels such as s are not cramped near the canvas edge.
Tune the overview layout to more closely match the reference proportions, with three large panels across the top and two similarly sized panels centered below.

demo_steps.narration: During the first full edge pass, only the late relaxations s→t and s→y improve distances, producing d[t]=6 and d[y]=7. The first gray predecessor edges show the best known one-edge paths from s.

demo_steps.title: Pass 2: propagate through t and y
demo_steps.narration: Now that t and y have finite estimates, their outgoing edges can improve other vertices. The algorithm reaches x with final estimate 4 through y→x and reaches z with estimate 2 through t→z.

demo_steps.title: Pass 3: a negative edge lowers t
demo_steps.narration: Because x is now known to have distance 4, relaxing x→t with weight −2 improves t from 6 down to 2. This shows why Bellman-Ford must keep making passes even after a vertex already has a finite estimate.

demo_steps.title: Pass 4: final improvement reaches z
demo_steps.narration: With t improved to 2, the next pass relaxes t→z with weight −4 and lowers z to −2. The final predecessor chain s→y→x→t→z is the shortest-path tree.

plan.keyInsight: Bellman-Ford works because each pass lets improved estimates travel one more edge along a shortest path, so even negative edges are handled as long as repeated relaxation is allowed to converge.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Use the same five-node layout as the textbook figure: s on the far left, t above y near the center, and x above z on the right. Draw all edges as thin black arrows with clear weight labels, including the paired curved arrows between t and x. Show distance estimates inside light-gray circular nodes. During code replay, flash the active edge; when relaxation succeeds, place a thick gray backing under that edge and update the destination node's number. Maintain a persistent gray predecessor-tree overlay after each successful update so the learner can see the evolving tree: first s→t and s→y, then y→x and t→z, then x→t replaces s→t, and finally t→z leads to z=−2. Include a pass/change counter beside the graph rather than recreating five static panels at once.
